newsitem.title: POLAND: Row erupts over bill to open secret Polish files.
newsitem.headline: Row erupts over bill to open secret Polish files.

text.p: Poland's ruling leftist coalition was enbroiled on Thursday in a bitter row over a bill that would open up secret interior ministry files to reveal former collaborators with the communist-era security police.

The Peasant Party (PSL) turned against its larger cabinet ally, the ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance (SLD), by backing the bill, which would set up a special court to examine whether candidates for top state posts had been agents.
The draft legislation was approved by a special parliamentary committee on Thursday after the PSL voted along with the right and centrist opposition to adopt it.

The bill looks set to trigger many heated disputes during the run-up to this year's parliamentary elections, but it seems unlikely to become law. The SLD said it would oppose it during its upcoming second reading in parliament.
President Aleksander Kwasniewski, a reformed communist, may veto the bill if parliament clears it in its current form, the president's top aide, Danuta Waniek, said.
The PSL and the opposition are short of the two-thirds majority needed to overturn presidential vetoes.
"My assessment of the bill in its current shape is critical. It serves as political revenge...and not reconciliation as the president wanted," Waniek told Reuters.

Waniek and the SLD said the bill would hamper the work of Poland's special services because it provided for unveiling former agents of the intelligence and counter-intelligence services and not just those of the political police.
SLD officials have said the bill was being used to discredit their party during the electoral campaign.

Poland, which overthrew the old administration in 1989, has failed to unmask former communist security police agents as has the Czech Republic and the former East Germany, where communist files were fully opened to the public.

Parties rooted in the Solidarity trade union did not address the problem when they held power until 1993. Most of them said the interior ministry's files, unverified and possibly forged, could embarrass innocent public figures.
The coalition of the ex-communists and the Peasant party, which is also rooted in the old system, buried the issue after it took over more than three years ago.

But Kwasniewski decided to reopen the case earlier this year after his political colleague, SLD leader Jozef Oleksy, was accused of having spied for Moscow. Prosecutors dropped the Olesky case probe, calling the evidence flawed and inadequate.
